comment.base: Federal obstruction of justice laws, primarily in 18 U.S. Code Chapter 73, prohibit interfering with government functions (courts, Congress, agencies) through acts like destroying evidence, witness tampering, bribery, or intimidation, with specific statutes covering court proceedings (18 U.S.C. § 1503), witnesses (18 U.S.C. § 1512), and agency/congressional inquiries (18 U.S.C. § 1505). These laws make it a crime to "corruptly" impede justice or proceedings, covering actions like hiding documents, lying, or threatening officials, with penalties ranging from fines to years in prison, depending on the severity and specific statute. Federal obstruction laws, primarily 18 U.S.C. § 1505, make it a crime to corruptly impede proceedings before federal agencies like ICE, including detention or deportation hearings, punishable by up to 5 years in prison; other statutes like 18 U.S.C. § 1510 cover obstructing investigations, and actions like hiding someone from arrest fall under other laws, meaning interfering with an ICE operation or officer is a serious federal offense, not just a local matter.Key Federal Statutes18 U.S.C. § 1505 (Obstruction of Proceedings): This law targets actions that corruptly or by force obstruct or impede due administration in federal agency proceedings, including those by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) (ICE).18 U.S.C. § 1510 (Obstruction of Criminal Investigations): This prohibits corruptly obstructing, influencing, or impeding a federal criminal investigation through bribery or other means, requiring intent to obstruct.18 U.S.C. § 1071 (Concealing a Fugitive): Making it illegal to harbor someone to prevent their discovery and arrest if a federal warrant exists.
